newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Greek Cypriots, police clash over peace concert.
newsitem.headline: Greek Cypriots, police clash over peace concert.

text.p: Greek Cypriots opposed to a United Nations-sponsored peace concert in the no-man's land dividing the island fought pitched battles with riot police on Monday in the streets of the capital, Nicosia.
Thirty people, including 15 policemen, were slightly injured during the sporadic clashes which went on for close to three hours. Thirty-seven people were arrested, police said.
"Their aim was to break through the roadblocks and to terrorise people. When that failed they resorted to all this hooliganism," police spokesman Glafcos Xenos told Reuters on Tuesday morning.

Opposition by Greek Cypriot groups to the free concert -- for both Turkish and Greek Cypriots -- was underlined by a protest concert in the Greek Cypriot-populated half of the capital which attracted about 5,000 people -- some 1,000 more than the estimated audience at the peace concert.

On the Turkish side, witnesses reported far-right Turkish "Grey Wolf" nationalists threw stones at a bus carrying a Turkish singer to join a Greek pop star at the peace concert. Windows were broken but there were no injuries, they said.
About 200 protesters, including motorcyclists, battled Greek Cypriot police in the business heart of their side of the capital.

Demonstrators smashed windows of police cars and threw at least two petrol bombs. Trash bins were set on fire and protesters lobbed stones at police -- a continuation of clashes that began before the concert with police protecting access to the concert site. Police responded with tear gas.
Police had mounted a massive security operation in the capital to ensure the concert remained peaceful. U.N. soldiers checked those entering and it passed off without incident.
Pop stars Burak Kut of Turkey and Sakis Rouvas of Greece sang for the crowd of young people in the U.N.-controlled no-man's land beside the Venetian walls that had once protected the city.
The aim was to break the ice, or begin to thaw it, between the youth of the island's two communities separated by years of enmity and mistrust.

Singing a mixture of Greek and Turkish songs, and several in English, the two singers drew cheers from a crowd as they hugged one another and shook hands at the end of the concert, which lasted about 90 minutes.
Turkey occupied northern Cyprus in 1974 in an invasion sparked by a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military then ruling Greece.
The concert took on a political meaning in the face of angry reactions from various groups on both sides of the divide.
"This conveyed a positive message to politicians to find a peaceful solution to this problem," said Rouvas at a news conference with Kut held immediately after the concert.
"I am sorry about some people who believe in what they are doing and resort to some means which cause disturbance," he said, referring to the incidents.
"In the long run this (concert) will have beneficial effects," Kut added.

The only hiccup to the concert, held in an abandoned football pitch, was when a Turkish member of the crowd lifted his arm and displayed the sign of the Grey Wolves group with his fingers. Witnesses said the spectator was escorted away from the site by U.N. soldiers.
A far-right Turkish nationalist group had driven around the Turkish section of Nicosia on Monday afternoon with loudspeakers publicising a protest meeting against the concert for the evening.
In the south, Greek Cypriot groups who saw the concert as an act of defeatism and Turkish propaganda announced their protest concert two km from the peace concert.
